extraction.Name: Hubert McClosky (deceased); affidavit given by Clara McClosky Lapointe (widow)
extraction.Refused/Protested: I know for sure that he did not apply for the patent and I also know that when his father, Frank McClosky brought the patent home to him, he even went so far to try to return it to the office and that he was told that as long as it was issued, he better keep it.
extraction.Sold/Mortgaged: He did mortgage it. Did not sell.
extraction.Buyer: Supposed to be for $2500. and paid interest on the loan for $2500. but the actual cash he received from the loan was $1800. The mortgagee for some reason held out $700.00, which to this day, has not been accounted for. In 1923 or 24, the Loan Company closed the mortgage.
extraction.Tax burden forced sale/Mortgage: The interest on this loan of $2500. on this land was a heavy weight on me after he died, and at various times, I tried to sell the land and pay off the note, but Judge Callender of Winner, absolutely refused to listen to my requests to sell... kept me paying interest on the land until I could not pay any more, then they took it away from me.
extraction.NOTES: Hubert McClosky died October 12, 1918. Left one child: Hubart Charles McClosky, 11 years old, who lives with Clara Lapointe. Affidavit given by widow Clara McClosky Lapointe, of legal age, sworn June 11, 1929 at Crow Agency, Montana before a Notary Public. McClosky's name was placed on a list of eligible patent recipients by agency employees without his application; his father Frank McClosky brought him the patent and he attempted to return it the next day. Mortgage loan was $2500 but only $1800 cash was actually received; $700 held out by mortgagee never accounted for. Judge Callender of Winner refused to allow sale of land, claiming to protect the minor heir, but ultimately worked in favor of mortgagees. Superintendent McGregor of Rosebud said he would look after the minor's interest but outcome unknown. Notary Public residing at Crow Agency, Montana; commission expires noted on document.
